name: District of Columbia Paid Family Leave
executionNotes: Executable with the frozen 2018 ACS DC/MD/VA place-of-work snapshots and reviewed pre-cutoff scenario. The population represents private employees in those three origins who report working in DC; smaller commuter origins and the statute's exact work-time test are not directly represented, so retrospective runs are methodology diagnostics rather than fresh validation.
forecastQuestion: Before tax collection began, how many total, parental, medical, and family claims would DC Paid Family Leave receive in its first operating year?
summary: Forecast claims and program operations immediately before employer tax collection began, using the enacted policy and only evidence available by the cutoff.

sources.title: Universal Paid Leave Amendment Act
sources._fix: URL repaired: subchapter IV-A returned 404 and does not exist; the provisions cited in the locator (SS 32-541.03 to 32-541.08) are in subchapter IV.

sources.title: Final Report on the Costs and Benefits of Paid Family and Medical Leave in the District of Columbia

sources.title: DC Paid Family Leave FY2021 Q4 Report
sources.locator: PFL Claim Type table: 8,430 parental; 2,901 medical; 848 family; 12,179 total

confounds: Benefits launched during the COVID-19 public health emergency.
The outcome window is approximately thirteen months rather than a standard program year.
Claims received are not identical to approved or paid claims.
evaluationDesign: Prospective forecast compared with later administrative counts; descriptive backtest, not a causal effect estimate.

verification.method: Every source URL was fetched and compared against the document it claims to be, and every scored figure was looked for in the source it cites.
findings: Claim counts 8,430 parental, 2,901 medical, 848 family and 12,179 total are exact, from Table 1 of the DOES FY21 Q4 report, and the manifest's window matches the report's own framing.
The statute URL returned 404 and was repaired: the Universal Paid Leave provisions are in subchapter IV, not IV-A.
The 2015 study's authorship was restored: Jeffrey Hayes, Institute for Women's Policy Research.
